parts.context: Two coordinators at a physiotherapy clinic are dealing with a problem with the clinic’s therapy pool.

lines: Owen, have you got a second? Facilities just emailed. The heater for the therapy pool failed overnight, and the water’s already down to twenty-two degrees.
Twenty-two? That’s far too cold for the knee group. They need it at thirty-two or so, or their joints just seize up. When can it be fixed?
That’s the problem. The replacement part has to come from a supplier in Winnipeg, and the technician said ten business days at the earliest. And our new six-week knee rehab group starts on Monday.

Twelve, actually. Someone was added yesterday from the surgical wait list. And most of them were discharged from hospital within the last three weeks, so the surgeon’s protocol is pretty strict: water-based exercise, starting no later than four weeks after the operation.
So pushing the whole group back two weeks isn’t really an option.

Not for most of them. For three or four of the patients who are further along, it wouldn’t matter much, but the others would be outside that window. And honestly, what worries me more is the referral side of things. Dr. Halvorsen’s office sends us almost half of our post-surgical patients. If we start bumping her people, she’ll start sending them to the hospital’s outpatient program instead.
Fair point. Have you heard from Mirela?

She’s on vacation until the twenty-first, but she answered my text. She said we can sort it out ourselves, as long as patients aren’t paying anything extra and we don’t sign anything longer than a month.
Okay. No extra costs for patients and no long contracts. That narrows things down a bit.

qs.q: Why can’t the clinic’s therapy pool be used for the new group?
o: The pool had to be drained after the heater failed.
The technician from Winnipeg cannot come until Monday.
A repair will not be finished before the program begins.
The surgeon has ruled out water exercise for the group.
qs.ev: the technician said ten business days at the earliest
qs.x: The part needs at least ten business days, but the group starts Monday, so the repair will not be ready in time. The part, not the technician, comes from Winnipeg, and nobody says the pool was drained.

qs.q: What worries Nadia most about postponing the group?
o: It could damage an important source of new patients.
Three or four patients would have to leave the group.
The surgeon would need to rewrite the exercise protocol.
Patients might have to pay for extra sessions later.
qs.ev: what worries me more is the referral side of things
qs.x: She says the referral side worries her more: the surgeon who sends half their patients might send them elsewhere. The three or four further-along patients could actually wait, so they would not have to leave.

qs.q: What has the clinic director told them?
o: To wait until she returns on the twenty-first
To charge patients a small fee if necessary
To sign a contract only if it is inexpensive
To find a short-term fix at no cost to patients
qs.ev: as long as patients aren’t paying anything extra and we don’t sign anything longer than a month
qs.x: Mirela lets them decide as long as patients pay nothing extra and any agreement lasts a month or less – a short-term, no-cost solution. She is away until the twenty-first but does not ask them to wait.

lines: What about the Bayview Aquatic Centre? It’s a city pool, and it’s only ten minutes from here.

I called them first thing. Their therapy pool is warm enough, but the only time they could give us is weekday mornings at seven. Half our group can’t drive yet, and the accessible transit service doesn’t start pickups until eight.
Right, so that’s out. What about the hotel downtown, the Harbourline? I know a personal trainer who uses their pool for private clients.
I looked into that too. They’d give us the pool for an hour every afternoon, which would be ideal, but they want a three-month minimum agreement and a fifteen-hundred-dollar deposit.
Three months. That breaks Mirela’s rule straight away.
Exactly. And frankly, the change rooms are up a full flight of stairs. For people who are three weeks out of knee surgery, that’s asking for trouble.
Okay, what if we just ran the first two weeks on land? Gentle range-of-motion work in our gym, and then we move into the pool once it’s fixed.
I suppose that could work for some of them, but the protocol specifically says water-based. I’d want Dr. Halvorsen to sign off before we change anything, and she’s in surgery all day.
Hmm. Oh, what about Maplecrest, the seniors’ residence on Alder Street? They put in a therapy pool last year, and I think their residents mostly use it in the mornings.
Maplecrest? I didn’t know they let outside groups use it.
I’m not sure they do, but my former colleague runs their recreation program. Let me give her a call right now.

qs.q: Why did Nadia reject the Bayview Aquatic Centre?
o: The water there is not warm enough for knee patients.
Many patients would have no way of arriving in time.
The pool is too far from the clinic for most of the group.
The only times available were on weekend mornings.
qs.ev: the accessible transit service doesn’t start pickups until eight
qs.x: The slot is at seven, but many patients cannot drive and accessible transit starts at eight, so they could not get there. She actually says the water is warm enough, and the pool is only ten minutes away.

qs.q: Apart from the length of the agreement, what problem does Nadia see with the Harbourline?
o: The pool is only available early in the morning.
Private clients use the pool every afternoon.
Patients would have to pay the deposit themselves.
Patients would struggle to reach the changing area.
qs.ev: the change rooms are up a full flight of stairs
qs.x: Stairs up to the change rooms are risky for people three weeks after knee surgery. The hotel actually offers afternoons, and the trainer’s private clients are mentioned only as how Owen knows the pool.

qs.q: How does Nadia feel about holding the first two weeks on land?
o: She sees some merit in it but wants approval first.
She prefers it to any of the pool options so far.
She rejects it because the gym is already booked.
She is confident that the surgeon would accept it.
qs.ev: I suppose that could work for some of them, but the protocol specifically says water-based.
qs.x: “I suppose that could work for some” is cautious partial agreement, and she wants the surgeon to sign off first. She never says she is confident the surgeon would agree, and the gym being booked is not mentioned.

lines: Okay, good news and slightly complicated news. Maplecrest will let us use their pool Monday, Wednesday and Friday from one-thirty to two-thirty, for four weeks.
Four weeks is fine. That’s within Mirela’s limit. What’s the complicated part?
They won’t charge us a rental fee, but in exchange they want one of our physios to run a free balance class for their residents once a week, for the same four weeks.
Huh. That’s actually not a bad trade. Priyanka has been asking to do more fall-prevention work, so I bet she’d jump at it. Anything else?
Just one thing. Their pool is only rated for ten people at a time.
And we have twelve. Okay, so we split them into two groups of six and run two back-to-back half-hour sessions?
We could, but half an hour is a lot shorter than the forty-five minutes in the protocol.

True. Hmm. What if the four patients who are furthest along, the ones who could have waited anyway, start on land in our gym this week and join everyone in the pool once ours is fixed? Then we’d only have eight in the water at Maplecrest.
But a minute ago you said you’d need Dr. Halvorsen’s approval for land work.
For the recent ones, yes. But for patients who are five or six weeks out, her protocol already allows land-based exercise. I checked it this morning.
Perfect. So eight in the pool at Maplecrest, four in our gym, and everyone back together here once the heater is replaced.
Great. I’ll draft a letter to the patients tonight. Can you check with Priyanka about the balance class before we promise Maplecrest anything?
I’ll catch her before her four o’clock appointment.

qs.q: What will the clinic provide in return for using Maplecrest’s pool?
o: A monthly rental fee paid by the clinic
Free assessments for the residence’s staff
Weekly sessions to help residents stay steady
Use of the clinic’s pool once it is repaired
qs.ev: they want one of our physios to run a free balance class for their residents once a week
qs.x: A weekly balance class for residents means sessions to keep them steady on their feet. Maplecrest explicitly will not charge a rental fee, and nothing is said about lending the clinic’s own pool.

qs.q: What have Nadia and Owen decided to do?
o: Run two shorter pool sessions of six patients each
Divide the group between two locations at first
Start all twelve patients on land for one week
Wait for the surgeon’s approval before starting
qs.ev: So eight in the pool at Maplecrest, four in our gym
qs.x: Eight patients will use Maplecrest’s pool and four will exercise in the clinic gym until the heater is replaced. The two half-hour sessions were suggested but dropped because they are shorter than the protocol requires.

parts.context: A man is speaking with a receptionist at a walk-in clinic.

lines: Hi there. I was hoping to see a doctor this morning. I’ve had a rash on my forearm for about four days, and it seems to be spreading.
Can I see your health card, please?
Here you go. Oh – wait. It says it expired last month. I completely forgot to renew it.

Unfortunately, the system won’t let me bill the province with an expired card, so you have two choices. You can pay as a private patient today, which is ninety-five dollars for a standard visit, and then send in the receipt once your card’s been renewed. Or you can renew it online right now. That usually goes through within an hour or two, and then we can register you as normal.
Ninety-five dollars. Would I definitely get that back?
In most cases, yes, as long as you renew within six months of the visit. But I’ll be honest with you: the reimbursement can take eight to ten weeks.
Hmm. And if I go and renew it, would I lose my place in line?

Not at all. The wait is about two and a half hours anyway. We use a virtual queue, so you don’t need to sit here. I’ll put your name down with your cell number, and you’ll get a text when you’re about thirty minutes from being seen. As long as your card is valid by the time you check back in, there’s no charge.
Oh, that’s handy. I was going to grab breakfast across the street anyway.
Go ahead. Just one thing: when the text comes, you need to reply within fifteen minutes. If you don’t, the system moves you to the end of the list.
Got it. Actually, my pharmacist mentioned that pharmacists can look at rashes now. Would that be quicker?

Pharmacists can assess some minor skin conditions, yes. But since yours is spreading, I’d honestly feel better if a doctor took a look. And if the area gets hot or you develop a fever, don’t wait for the text – go straight to emergency.
No fever. It’s just itchy. Okay, let’s do the virtual queue, and I’ll renew the card over breakfast.
Perfect. What’s the best number to text you at?
Oh no. My phone’s at four percent. Could you call me instead?
I’m afraid the system can only send texts. But there’s a free charging station over by the water fountain, if you have your cable.
I do, actually. I’ll sit here and charge it for a few minutes before I head out, then.

qs.q: Why can’t Tomasz be registered in the usual way?
o: He left his health card at home.
The clinic’s billing system is down.
He has never visited this clinic before.
His coverage document is out of date.
qs.ev: It says it expired last month.
qs.x: His health card expired last month, so the clinic cannot bill the province. He did hand over the card, so it was not left at home, and the system works – it just rejects expired cards.

qs.q: What does the receptionist suggest about paying as a private patient?
o: He would lose the money if he renewed online.
He would be repaid, but not for some time.
It would allow him to see a doctor sooner.
It costs more than a normal provincial visit.
qs.ev: the reimbursement can take eight to ten weeks
qs.x: She says he would usually be reimbursed but warns it takes eight to ten weeks. Paying privately does not shorten the two-and-a-half-hour wait, so it would not get him seen sooner.

qs.q: What happens if a patient does not answer the text quickly enough?
o: They lose their place and must wait longer.
They are charged the private-patient fee.
They must register again at the front desk.
The receptionist phones them instead.
qs.ev: the system moves you to the end of the list
qs.x: Missing the fifteen-minute reply window sends the patient to the end of the list, so they wait longer. The receptionist later says the system can only text, so phoning is not an option.

qs.q: What is the receptionist’s opinion about seeing a pharmacist instead?
o: It would be quicker and equally appropriate.
Pharmacists cannot deal with skin problems.
His symptoms call for a doctor’s assessment.
It is only sensible if he develops a fever.
qs.ev: since yours is spreading, I’d honestly feel better if a doctor took a look
qs.x: Because the rash is spreading, she would “feel better if a doctor took a look”. She agrees pharmacists can assess some minor skin conditions, and a fever would mean going to emergency, not a pharmacy.

qs.q: What will Tomasz most likely do next?
o: Stay at the clinic briefly to power up his phone
Cross the street to have breakfast immediately
Pay the private fee so that he is seen sooner
Give the receptionist a work phone number
qs.ev: I’ll sit here and charge it for a few minutes before I head out, then.
qs.x: His phone is almost dead and texts are the only option, so he will charge it at the clinic first. Breakfast comes later, after he heads out.

parts.context: A woman is calling a hospital’s caregiver support line.

lines: Caregiver Support Line, this is Ravi speaking. How can I help you today?

Hi, my name is Danielle. My father has moderate dementia, and he’s been living with us since last spring. I’ve been looking after him full-time, and honestly, I’m exhausted. A nurse at his memory clinic gave me this number and said you might have some kind of break program.

I’m really glad you called. Yes, we coordinate a few respite options. The most popular one is our adult day program at the Eastgate Community Health Centre. It runs Tuesdays and Thursdays from nine-thirty to three-thirty. Participants do gentle exercise, music, memory games, and they get a hot lunch.
That sounds wonderful. What does it cost?

The daily fee is twenty-eight dollars, and that includes lunch. If you need us to pick him up, the accessible van is six dollars each way. Now, if your household income is under a certain level, the fee can be reduced, sometimes all the way to zero, but you’d need to send us last year’s tax assessment.
Okay. Could he start next week?

Unfortunately, not quite that fast. Before anyone joins, a care coordinator has to do a home assessment, mainly to make sure the program is a good fit, for example, whether he’s comfortable in a group setting. At the moment, the wait for that visit is about three weeks. After that, there’s usually a space within a few days.
Three weeks. Hmm. Is there anything sooner, even just for a weekend? My sister’s getting married in Halifax at the end of next month, and I really need to be there.

For that, you’d want our short-stay respite beds at Linden Grove, which is a long-term care home. Families can book up to thirty nights a year, at forty-two dollars a night. But – and this is important – bookings have to be made at least fourteen days in advance, and the same home assessment is required first.
So the assessment is really the key to everything.
Exactly. I’d recommend we book it today. I can also mark it as a priority because of the wedding date. I can’t promise anything, but that sometimes moves people up by a week or so.
Yes, please do that. And is there anything for me in the meantime?

There is. We run a free six-week workshop for caregivers on Wednesday evenings, from seven to eight-thirty. It covers things like handling agitation and planning for the future. You can join in person or online, and if you come in person, a volunteer can sit with your father in the room next door.
Oh, that’s thoughtful. I think online would be easier for me, though, since my husband’s home in the evenings.
No problem at all. I’ll email you the link. Now, let me just get your father’s health card number so I can book that assessment.

qs.q: Why is Danielle calling?
o: To book a memory assessment for her father
To find a way to take time off from caregiving
To arrange transport to her father’s clinic
To complain about advice from a clinic nurse
qs.ev: said you might have some kind of break program
qs.x: She is exhausted from full-time care and asks about a “break program” – a way to get relief. The memory clinic nurse only gave her the number; she is not complaining or booking a memory test.

qs.q: What is true about the fee for the day program?
o: It includes the cost of the accessible van.
It is charged for each half-day attended.
It can be lowered depending on family income.
It must be paid before the home assessment.
qs.ev: if your household income is under a certain level, the fee can be reduced
qs.x: The $28 fee can be reduced, even to zero, for lower-income households. The van is a separate charge of six dollars each way, so it is not included in the fee.

qs.q: What must happen before her father can use either service?
o: He must attend a trial day at Eastgate.
Danielle must send last year’s tax assessment.
His memory clinic must send a referral.
Someone must visit to check he is suitable.
qs.ev: a care coordinator has to do a home assessment
qs.x: Both the day program and the respite beds require a home assessment by a care coordinator. The tax assessment is needed only to reduce the fee, not to join.

qs.q: Why does Danielle ask whether anything is available sooner?
o: She needs to travel for a family celebration.
Her husband will soon be away on business.
Her father’s condition has suddenly worsened.
The day program is full for three weeks.
qs.ev: My sister’s getting married in Halifax at the end of next month
qs.x: Her sister’s wedding in Halifax means she must travel. The three-week wait is for the assessment visit, not because the day program is full.

qs.q: What does Ravi suggest about marking the request as a priority?
o: It will guarantee an assessment next week.
It only applies to short-stay bed bookings.
It may speed things up, but not for certain.
It will reduce the booking notice to a week.
qs.ev: I can’t promise anything, but that sometimes moves people up by a week or so.
qs.x: “Can’t promise” plus “sometimes” means it might help but is not guaranteed. The fourteen-day notice for respite beds is a separate rule that the priority flag does not change.

qs.q: How will Danielle most likely take part in the workshop?
o: In person, while a volunteer stays with her father
From home, while her husband is with her father
In person, accompanied by her husband
By phone on Wednesday afternoons
qs.ev: I think online would be easier for me, though, since my husband’s home in the evenings
qs.x: She chooses online because her husband is home in the evenings to be with her father. The volunteer option applies only to people who attend in person, which she decides against.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about a regional health program.

lines: Good evening. A program that sends paramedics to check on older adults in their homes, before there’s an emergency, will be expanded across the Fenwick Valley region starting in January. The Community Paramedicine Program began two years ago as a pilot in just three rural townships. Under the program, paramedics who are not assigned to ambulances visit patients who have called 911 or gone to hospital repeatedly. They check blood pressure and blood sugar, review medications and look for hazards in the home, such as loose rugs or poor lighting. According to the regional health authority, 911 calls from enrolled patients fell by about a third during the pilot, although officials caution that the pilot group was small, fewer than two hundred people. The expansion will bring the program to all eleven municipalities in the region and add eighteen paramedic positions. It’s being paid for through a three-year provincial grant worth four-point-two million dollars. Paramedic supervisor Colleen Ferris helped design the pilot.

Honestly, what surprised us most wasn’t the medical side at all. It was loneliness. A lot of these folks were calling 911 because nobody else was checking on them. Once they knew we’d be coming every second Tuesday, the calls just settled down. But we also caught some serious problems early. One gentleman had been taking a double dose of his heart medication for weeks, because two different pharmacies were filling the same prescription.

Not everyone is convinced the model will work as well in larger towns. The union representing paramedics says it supports the program in principle, but worries that during busy periods the new positions will be pulled back onto ambulances. The health authority says the eighteen positions will be dedicated to home visits and protected in the contract. Residents can’t sign themselves up for the program. Referrals must come from a family doctor, a hospital discharge planner or a home-care nurse. The first visits under the expanded program are expected in the region’s northern towns in early February, with the remaining municipalities to follow by summer.

qs.q: What is the news report mainly about?
o: The wider rollout of a preventive home-visit service
A plan to shorten ambulance response times
A shortage of paramedics in rural townships
A program that delivers medication to seniors
qs.ev: will be expanded across the Fenwick Valley region starting in January
qs.x: The report covers the region-wide expansion of paramedic home visits meant to prevent emergencies. Medications are reviewed during visits, not delivered, and response times are never discussed.

qs.q: What do officials suggest about the results of the pilot?
o: They showed hospital visits fell by two-thirds.
They will be tested again before the expansion.
They were stronger in towns than in rural areas.
They are promising but come from a small sample.
qs.ev: officials caution that the pilot group was small
qs.x: Calls fell by about a third, but officials caution that fewer than two hundred people took part, so the result is encouraging yet limited. The figure was one third of 911 calls, not two-thirds of hospital visits.

qs.q: According to Colleen Ferris, what was unexpected about the pilot?
o: Most patients turned out to have heart conditions.
Many patients called mainly because they were lonely.
Pharmacies were too slow when filling repeat prescriptions.
Patients asked for visits more than twice a month.
qs.ev: It was loneliness.
qs.x: She says what surprised them most was loneliness: people called 911 because no one checked on them. The heart medication story involved one man and a duplicate prescription, not slow pharmacies.

qs.q: What concern has the paramedics’ union raised?
o: The provincial grant ends after only three years.
Paramedics are not trained to review medications.
Home-visit staff could be reassigned to emergencies.
Larger towns will receive fewer new positions.
qs.ev: worries that during busy periods the new positions will be pulled back onto ambulances
qs.x: The union fears the new home-visit paramedics will be moved back onto ambulances when things get busy. The three-year grant is mentioned as the funding source, not as a union complaint.

qs.q: How can a resident join the program?
o: By calling 911 more than twice in one year
By registering with their own municipality
By applying online starting in February
Through a recommendation from a health worker
qs.ev: Referrals must come from a family doctor, a hospital discharge planner or a home-care nurse.
qs.x: Residents cannot sign up themselves; a doctor, discharge planner or home-care nurse must refer them. February is when the first visits start in the north, not when online applications open.

parts.context: Three managers at a distribution company are discussing next year’s employee wellness budget.

lines: Okay, let’s get started. We have forty thousand dollars in the wellness budget for next year, and last year most of it went to gym subsidies. The staff survey results are in, and, well, they’re not what I expected.
Let me guess. Nobody used the gym memberships.
Not nobody. But only about fifteen percent of staff claimed the subsidy, and almost all of them were office employees. On the warehouse floor, it was under five percent.
Which makes sense, really. If you’ve been lifting boxes for ten hours, the last thing you want is a spin class.
Exactly. My people don’t need more exercise. They need their backs to stop hurting. We had nine lost-time injuries last year, and seven of them were strains – shoulders, lower backs.
That matches the survey. The top request from warehouse staff was physiotherapy, and the second was better lifting equipment.
Equipment isn’t really wellness, though. That should come out of the operations budget.
In theory, sure. But the operations budget is frozen until the new conveyor is paid off, so in practice, if it doesn’t come from wellness, it doesn’t happen.
I hear you, but I’m not comfortable moving money from one budget to plug a hole in another. The auditors flagged exactly that kind of thing last year.

Let’s park equipment for a moment. What about an on-site physiotherapist? I got a quote from Clearwater Physio. A physio would come in two half-days a week, do assessments, teach lifting technique and treat minor strains before they turn into injuries.

That’s a big chunk. What’s left for everyone else? The office staff’s top request was mental health support, not gym passes. Our employee assistance plan only covers three counselling sessions, and people say that’s barely enough to get started.
Raising it to eight sessions per person would cost roughly eleven thousand, based on last year’s usage.
So twenty-six plus eleven is thirty-seven. That leaves three thousand.
It would have to go, or at least be cut back dramatically.
Honestly, I wouldn’t miss it, but I suspect a few people in the office would make some noise.
They might, but fifteen percent uptake isn’t much of a case. Here’s what worries me about the physio, though. Is there any evidence it actually reduces injuries, or are we just hoping?
Clearwater sent me data from two other warehouses. Strain injuries dropped by about forty percent in the first year. Of course, they’re selling something, so I’d take that with a grain of salt.
Even half of that would pay for itself. Each lost-time injury costs us something like eight thousand in overtime and premiums.
Okay, that’s a fair argument. If we prevent even three injuries, we’re ahead. But I want it as a one-year pilot with clear numbers, not a permanent commitment.
That’s reasonable. Dev, can you track strain injuries every month?
I already do. But what about the remaining three thousand?
What if we keep a small version of the gym subsidy? Say, a fifty-dollar reimbursement for anything active, not just gyms. Skates, hiking boots, a yoga app.
Three thousand at fifty dollars only covers sixty people. We have over two hundred.

First come, first served, then. It’s better than nothing, and it’s fairer than last year, because warehouse staff could use it too, for things like work boots. Well, no, not work boots. That’s safety equipment.
Fine. Physio as a one-year pilot, counselling up to eight sessions, and the fifty-dollar activity reimbursement with whatever’s left. I’ll draft the budget memo.
And I’ll let Clearwater know we’re in, on a twelve-month contract.

qs.q: What did the survey show about last year’s gym subsidy?
o: Warehouse staff used it more than office staff.
About fifteen percent of warehouse staff claimed it.
Few people used it, especially outside the office.
Most staff wanted spin classes added to it.
qs.ev: On the warehouse floor, it was under five percent.
qs.x: Only fifteen percent of all staff used it, and under five percent of warehouse workers. The fifteen percent figure was for the whole company, not the warehouse.

qs.q: Why does Fiona think the gym results make sense?
o: Warehouse work is already physically tiring.
The gyms are too far from the warehouse.
Office employees have more free time.
The subsidy did not cover spin classes.
qs.ev: If you’ve been lifting boxes for ten hours, the last thing you want is a spin class.
qs.x: She means people who do heavy physical work all day do not want more exercise afterwards. The spin class is just her example; she does not say the subsidy excluded it.

qs.q: Why does Dev want equipment paid for out of the wellness budget?
o: The auditors recommended it last year.
The usual source of funding is unavailable.
Equipment would cost less than a physio.
Wellness money cannot be spent on injuries.
qs.ev: the operations budget is frozen until the new conveyor is paid off
qs.x: Equipment normally comes from operations, but that budget is frozen, so wellness is the only option in practice. The auditors are mentioned by Fiona as a reason against the idea.

qs.q: Why does Fiona object to Dev’s suggestion about equipment?
o: She doubts equipment would prevent strains.
Warehouse staff never asked for equipment.
The conveyor has made equipment unnecessary.
It could create problems with financial reviews.
qs.ev: The auditors flagged exactly that kind of thing last year.
qs.x: She is uncomfortable shifting money between budgets because auditors criticized it before. Equipment was actually the warehouse staff’s second request, so they did ask for it.

qs.q: How does Hélène regard the figures from Clearwater?
o: As proof that the physio will pay for itself
As possibly exaggerated given their source
As irrelevant because the warehouses differ
As likely to underestimate the benefits
qs.ev: they’re selling something, so I’d take that with a grain of salt
qs.x: “Take that with a grain of salt” because Clearwater is “selling something” means she suspects the numbers are inflated. It is Dev, not Hélène, who argues the physio would pay for itself.

qs.q: What finally convinces Fiona to support the physiotherapist?
o: Even a modest drop in injuries would save money.
Clearwater offered to lower its annual price.
The survey ranked physio first among all staff.
Dev agreed to begin tracking injuries monthly.
qs.ev: Each lost-time injury costs us something like eight thousand in overtime and premiums.
qs.x: After Dev explains that each injury costs about $8,000, Fiona says preventing even three puts them ahead. Dev already tracks injuries, and physio was top only for warehouse staff.

qs.q: What condition does Fiona set for the physiotherapy plan?
o: Counselling must remain at three sessions.
The gym subsidy must be kept in full.
The physio must visit more often than planned.
It must be temporary and closely measured.
qs.ev: I want it as a one-year pilot with clear numbers
qs.x: A one-year pilot with clear numbers is a temporary, measured trial. Counselling is actually being increased to eight sessions, and the gym subsidy is being cut back.

qs.q: What will happen to the money that is left over?
o: It will buy safety boots for warehouse staff.
It will fund gym passes for office workers.
It will partly repay some staff for activity costs.
It will add three more counselling sessions.
qs.ev: a fifty-dollar reimbursement for anything active
qs.x: The last $3,000 becomes a first-come $50 reimbursement for active purchases, covering about sixty people. Work boots were mentioned but immediately ruled out as safety equipment.

parts.context: You will hear a radio report about doctors referring patients to community activities.

lines: When seventy-four-year-old Bernard Okafor went to see his family doctor last spring about poor sleep and low mood, he expected to leave with a prescription for pills. Instead, he left with a referral to a weekly woodworking group at his local community centre. Bernard is one of several thousand patients in the province who have taken part in what’s known as social prescribing – a practice in which doctors, nurses and social workers connect patients with non-medical activities such as art classes, walking groups, gardening or volunteering. Supporters say it tackles something medicine has long overlooked: many of the problems that bring people into clinics are rooted in loneliness, inactivity and stress. Dr. Lionel Achterberg, a family physician in a mid-sized city, has been writing these referrals for three years.

I’m not throwing out medication. Some patients absolutely need it. But I’d say a quarter of my appointments are with people whose main problem is that they’re isolated. Writing a prescription for an antidepressant takes thirty seconds. Connecting someone to a choir actually changes their week.

A provincial evaluation found that participants reported better mood and fewer visits to their doctor after six months. But critics say the evidence is thinner than the enthusiasm suggests. Many of the studies are small, rely on patients’ own reports and have no comparison group. As one health economist put it to me, people who agree to join a choir may simply be the ones who were already ready to get better. There’s also a practical problem. Social prescribing depends on community programs, and those programs often run on tiny budgets and volunteer energy. In some rural areas, doctors say there is simply nothing to refer patients to. One clinic manager told me her team referred thirty patients to a walking group that was cancelled two months later, when its volunteer leader moved away. Then there’s the question of cost. Most community programs charge small fees, and for low-income patients, even ten dollars a week can be a barrier. Some regions now employ link workers – staff who help patients find activities and actually get there – but those positions are often funded year by year. Dr. Achterberg acknowledges the gaps, and says referrals without support can do more harm than good.

The worst thing we could do is hand someone a pamphlet and call it care. If there’s no link worker, no follow-up, and the program falls apart, then frankly we’ve just made a lonely person feel rejected twice.

As for Bernard, he now spends Tuesday mornings building birdhouses. He says he’s sleeping better and has made two new friends, one of whom now drives him to the group, although he admits he’s not sure whether it’s the woodworking or the coffee and conversation afterwards. “Does it matter?” he asks.

p1.meta: From: Yasmin Haddad | To: Corinne Leblanc | Subject: Finally certified (and a favour to ask)
p1.text:
Hi Corinne,

I hope the new unit is treating you well and that the night shifts have finally eased off. I owe you a proper catch-up, but I wanted to tell you my news first: I passed my community nutrition educator exam! After two failed attempts at the practical component, I’d honestly started to wonder whether I was kidding myself, so when the results came through on Friday, I actually cried in the grocery store parking lot.

The timing couldn’t be better. You remember the Thursday cooking group I’ve been helping with at the Riverside Neighbourhood House? The coordinator, Abdi, is moving to Calgary in December, and the board has asked me to take over. It’s mostly newcomer families, many of them dealing with type 2 diabetes or high blood pressure for the first time, and a lot of them find Canadian grocery stores overwhelming. Everything comes in boxes, the portions are huge, and the labels might as well be written in code.

So here’s my plan. Starting in January, I want to turn the group into an eight-week series. Each week we’d cook one affordable meal together, and I’d add a short practical lesson: reading labels, stretching a budget, swapping ingredients without losing the flavours people grew up with. The board has approved a small budget for groceries, but not for guest speakers.

Which brings me to the favour. Would you be willing to lead one session on managing blood sugar? You explain things so clearly, without making anyone feel lectured, and I think hearing it from a nurse would carry more weight than hearing it from me. It would be about forty-five minutes, and you could pick whichever Thursday suits your schedule. I know it would be unpaid, so please don’t feel any pressure. I’d completely understand if you’d rather keep your days off for yourself.

Also, Abdi warned me that the kitchen’s oven runs hot, so if you have any recipes that work in a slow cooker, send them my way!

Let me know what you think. And dinner’s on me next time either way – I mean it.

Hugs,
Yasmin

p3.title: Into the Cold: The Rise of Winter Swimming Clubs
paras: When the Polar Ripples Swim Club was founded in 2019, it had six members who met on an empty beach every Sunday morning in January. Today it has more than three hundred, and similar clubs have appeared on lakes and ocean inlets from coastal British Columbia to Nova Scotia. Members describe the experience in almost spiritual terms: the shock of the first plunge, the burning skin and then, a minute or two later, a sense of calm that can last the entire day. Club organizer Teresa Lindgren says most newcomers arrive after reading about the mental-health benefits online, but they stay for the company. “Nobody does this alone,” she says. “The cold strips away your small talk. You end up knowing people very well, very quickly.” Many members say they had never swum outdoors before joining.

Researchers are more cautious. Brief cold-water immersion does trigger a sharp release of stress hormones, followed by a rebound in mood-related chemicals, which may explain the calm that swimmers report. Small studies have linked regular winter swimming to reduced fatigue and improved mood, but most involved fewer than fifty participants, and almost all were people who chose to swim, which makes it difficult to separate the effect of the water from the effect of being the kind of person who enjoys this sort of challenge. “I’m not saying the benefits are imaginary,” says physiologist Dr. Mikael Varga. “I’m saying we don’t yet know how much of it is the cold and how much is the friendship, the fresh air and the sense of accomplishment.” Claims that cold water strengthens the immune system remain largely unproven.

Doctors also stress that the risks are real. The most dangerous moment is not hypothermia, which takes considerably longer to develop than most people assume, but the first minute in the water, when the body’s cold shock response causes involuntary gasping and a sudden spike in heart rate and blood pressure. For people with undiagnosed heart conditions, this reaction can be fatal. Swimmers can also lose strength in their hands and arms within ten minutes, making it hard to climb out. For this reason, experienced swimmers recommend entering slowly, never diving in, and staying close to shore. Anyone with heart disease, high blood pressure or asthma is advised to talk to a doctor before trying it, and drinking alcohol beforehand is strongly discouraged.

Most established clubs now have written safety rules. At Polar Ripples, first-timers must attend a short orientation and are paired with an experienced “buddy” for their first three swims. Swims are cancelled if the wind exceeds forty kilometres an hour or if ice has formed more than a few metres from shore. In their first season, members are asked to stay in for no more than one minute per degree of water temperature – so about four minutes in four-degree water. Volunteers keep thermoses of hot water and spare blankets on shore, and the club has partnered with a local paddling shop that lends neoprene gloves and booties free of charge. The annual membership fee of twenty dollars covers insurance and the club’s first-aid supplies.

p4.title: Menu Calorie Counts Are Feeding Us the Wrong Message
p4.byline: Opinion | by Lorna Bettencourt, registered dietitian
p4.text:
Three years ago, our province began requiring restaurant chains with twenty or more locations to post calorie counts on their menus. The idea was simple and, I admit, appealing: give people information at the moment they decide what to eat, and they will make healthier choices. As a dietitian, I supported the policy at the time. I no longer do.

Start with the evidence. When researchers have compared what people order before and after calorie labels appear, the results are modest at best. The most optimistic studies find that customers order perhaps thirty to fifty fewer calories per meal – roughly the equivalent of a single cookie spread across an entire lunch. Several well-designed studies have found no measurable change at all. People who already pay attention to nutrition use the numbers; people who don’t, mostly don’t.

That might be acceptable if the labels were harmless. They are not. For the significant number of Canadians living with eating disorders, a menu covered in numbers can turn a meal with friends into an exercise in anxiety. Several of my clients who are in recovery have told me they now avoid restaurants entirely. That is a real cost, and it was barely discussed when the policy was designed.

My deeper objection, however, is that calorie counts send the wrong message about what healthy eating means. A calorie number tells you nothing about whether a dish contains vegetables, fibre or protein, or whether it contains half a day’s worth of salt. Under the current system, a 450-calorie bowl of instant noodles looks like a better choice than a 650-calorie plate of salmon, rice and greens. We have spent decades teaching people to think about food as nourishment, and then we put a single number on every menu that encourages them to think of it as arithmetic.

To be fair, the policy has had one benefit its supporters rarely mention. Faced with the prospect of printing 1,200 next to their signature burger, several chains quietly reformulated their recipes or introduced smaller portions. Those changes help everyone, including people who never look at a menu board. But this was a side effect, and there are more direct ways to achieve it.

What would work better? First, sodium warnings. Most Canadians eat far more salt than they need, and restaurant meals are a major source. A simple symbol next to dishes with very high sodium would flag the meals that are genuinely concerning, without asking customers to do math. Second, portion choices. Restaurants should be required to offer smaller sizes of their main dishes at a lower price. Many people would happily eat less if they weren’t paying for a plate designed for a lumberjack. Third, the province should work directly with the restaurant industry to set voluntary targets for reducing salt and sugar, with public reporting of who meets them.

None of these ideas is perfect, and I am not suggesting we tear down every calorie label tomorrow. Some people find them genuinely useful, and they should remain available on request or online. But when the province reviews the policy next spring, I hope it asks a better question than “Do people see the numbers?” It should ask, “Are people eating better?” On that question, the answer so far is no.

t1.model:
Dear Program Coordinator,

I am writing about the Tuesday and Thursday evening Healthy Back program at Elmwood Recreation Centre, for which I paid $240 in September.

For the first four weeks, the classes were excellent. Our original instructor kept the group small, demonstrated every movement slowly and offered gentler versions for participants with chronic pain. Since she left, however, the program has changed considerably. The new instructor moves at a much faster pace, has added jumping exercises and weighted twists, and rarely corrects anyone’s form.

Unfortunately, this has affected me directly. I joined on my physiotherapist’s advice after a disc injury, and over the past two weeks my lower back pain has returned to where it was in the summer. I have missed three classes and paid for an extra physiotherapy appointment myself.

I would therefore ask the centre either to restore the original low-impact format or to refund the remaining six weeks, which I calculate to be $120. I would also appreciate it if the new instructor were reminded that many participants are recovering from injuries.

Sincerely,
Alan Pereira

t2.intro: Your employer has set aside money to support employees’ health next year and is asking staff to choose between two options. Only one option can be funded.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer? Explain the reasons for your choice.
t2.a: Option A: An on-site fitness room with exercise equipment, open from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., plus two free group classes a week led by a qualified trainer.
t2.b: Option B: A personal wellness account of $500 per employee per year that can be spent on approved items such as gym memberships, sports equipment, massage or nutrition counselling.
t2.model:
I would prefer Option B, the personal wellness account, mainly because healthy habits look very different from one employee to the next.

An on-site fitness room would certainly be convenient, and I can see why it appeals to colleagues who already enjoy working out before or after their shifts. However, it would mainly benefit one type of employee. People with young children, long commutes or injuries are unlikely to use a gym at the office, yet the company would be spending their share of the budget on it.

A $500 account, by contrast, lets each person invest in what actually works for them. A colleague recovering from a back injury could put it toward massage therapy, while someone managing diabetes might book sessions with a dietitian. Personally, I would use it for a community pool pass, since swimming is the only exercise my knees tolerate.

I admit that the account requires more paperwork, and some people may not use it at all. Still, a benefit that employees choose for themselves is far more likely to change behaviour than equipment that sits unused in a basement room.

t1.prompt: Your friend has just been told by their doctor that their blood pressure is too high. They feel stressed about it and do not know where to start. Give your friend some advice about how to improve their health.
t1.model: I’m really sorry you’re dealing with this, but honestly, the fact that your doctor caught it early is good news. High blood pressure is really common, and small changes can make a big difference. First, I’d start with salt, because that’s probably the easiest win. You’d be surprised how much is hidden in things like bread, soup and takeout, so maybe try cooking at home a few more nights a week and checking labels when you shop. Second, get moving, but don’t go overboard. You don’t need to train for a marathon. A brisk thirty-minute walk after dinner most days would be a great start, and I’d happily join you a couple of times a week if you want company. Third, look at your stress and your sleep. I know work has been brutal lately, and that really does affect your blood pressure. Even ten minutes of breathing exercises before bed could help. Finally, buy a home blood pressure monitor. They’re not expensive, and tracking your numbers will show you what’s working and give your doctor better information. Just don’t try to change everything in one week. Pick one or two things, stick with them, and build from there.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you or someone you know had to recover from an illness or an injury. What happened, and what did you learn from the experience?
t2.model: About three years ago, I slipped on black ice outside my apartment and broke my wrist. I needed surgery, and for six weeks my arm was in a cast, which was a nightmare because I’m right-handed and I couldn’t even tie my shoes. The hardest part, though, came after the cast was removed. My wrist was so stiff that I couldn’t turn a doorknob, so I went to physiotherapy twice a week for three months. Honestly, I was impatient, and at one point I skipped my home exercises for a whole week, and my progress went right backwards. My physiotherapist was pretty blunt with me about it. What I learned is that recovery is mostly about consistency, not big efforts. Ten minutes of boring exercises every day did more for me than anything else. And now I always buy ice cleats in November.

scene.alt: An outdoor community health fair in a sunny park. A blue banner across the top reads “COMMUNITY HEALTH FAIR”. On the left, under a red-and-white striped booth labelled “BLOOD PRESSURE”, a nurse in a white top with her hair in a bun stands beside an older man with grey hair and glasses in an orange shirt, who is sitting on a chair. In the middle, a woman with curly hair in a green shirt stands near a wooden table holding a tray of orange fruit slices. On the right, a woman in a purple dress is stretching with both arms raised, and a young girl in a yellow shirt copies her, next to a sign reading “FREE YOGA 2 PM”. In the foreground, a man in a teal shirt walks an orange dog on a leash. There are trees, a cloud and a bright sun.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This picture shows a community health fair in a park on a bright, sunny day. There’s a big blue banner across the top that says “Community Health Fair”. On the left, there’s a booth with a red-and-white striped roof and a sign that says “Blood Pressure”. A nurse, I think, in a white top with her hair in a bun, is standing there, and an older man with grey hair and glasses is sitting on a chair next to her, probably waiting to have his blood pressure checked. In the middle, a woman with curly hair is holding a tray of what look like orange slices, maybe free healthy snacks. On the right, a woman in a purple dress is stretching with both arms up, and a little girl in yellow is copying her. In front, a man is walking his orange dog.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the yoga session on the right is going to get a lot bigger very soon. The sign says free yoga at two o’clock, and the woman in the purple dress is probably the instructor warming up. The little girl is already copying her, so I imagine her parents will wander over, and more people from the fair will join in on the grass. Meanwhile, the nurse will probably put the cuff on the older man’s arm and check his blood pressure. If the reading is a bit high, she might give him a pamphlet and suggest he see his doctor. As for the man with the dog, I think the dog will smell the fruit and pull him straight toward the woman with the tray, and she’ll probably offer him a sample. Hopefully the dog won’t knock anything over!

t5.intro: Your family wants to start a regular weekend activity together to become more active. You have found two options. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a family member that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

options.title: Family swim pass – Rivergate Aquatic Centre
details: $65 per month for the whole family
Open swim Saturday and Sunday, 1–4 p.m.

options.title: Indoor climbing gym – family intro course

other.title: Saturday trail hiking club
details: Cancelled in heavy rain or snow

t5.persuade: Your brother prefers the Saturday trail hiking club. Persuade him that your choice is better.
t5.model: I get why the hiking club appeals to you – it’s cheap, and being outdoors is great. But I really think the climbing course is the better choice for us. First, it’s a five-minute walk from home. With the hiking club, we could spend up to two hours in the car every Saturday, which kind of defeats the purpose of an active weekend. Second, hikes get cancelled in heavy rain or snow, and around here that could mean half the winter. The climbing gym is indoors, so we’d actually stick with it. Third, the course includes a real instructor and all the equipment, so we’d learn proper skills safely. Yes, two hundred and twenty dollars is more than forty, but once you add gas for those long drives, the difference isn’t that big. And the kids would love it.

t6.situation: Your father had a stroke last year and can no longer drive. After waiting four months, he finally has an appointment with a specialist next Wednesday morning, and you promised to drive him and stay with him. Today, your manager told you that an important client meeting has been moved to Wednesday morning and that she expects you to give the presentation.
options: Talk to your father and explain that you need to reschedule the appointment or find someone else to take him.
Talk to your manager and explain why you cannot give the presentation on Wednesday morning.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hi Grace, do you have a few minutes? It’s about the client meeting next Wednesday. I completely understand how important this account is, and I really appreciate you trusting me with the presentation. The problem is that I promised to drive my father to a specialist appointment that same morning. He waited four months for it, and since his stroke he can’t drive and gets confused in unfamiliar places, so I really need to be with him. If he misses it, the next opening could be months away. That said, I don’t want to leave the team in a difficult spot. I could finish the slides by Monday and walk Jordan through them, since he knows the client well. Or, if the client is flexible, I could join by video for the key section. I hope you understand.

t7.prompt: Some people think the government should add a special tax to sugary drinks, such as soft drinks and energy drinks, and use the money for health programs. Others think this is unfair to consumers. What is your opinion? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: I’m in favour of a tax on sugary drinks, as long as the money is clearly used for health programs. My first reason is that these drinks are a major source of empty calories, especially for kids and teenagers. A large soft drink can contain more sugar than a person should have in an entire day, and there’s no real nutritional benefit. If a tax makes those drinks a little more expensive, some people will switch to water or milk, and over time that could reduce problems like type 2 diabetes and tooth decay. Second, the tax could pay for things that genuinely help communities, like free sports programs, nutrition classes in schools or water fountains in parks. That way, the money goes straight back into prevention. I do understand the argument that it’s unfair, because lower-income families tend to spend a larger share of their budget on these drinks. But that’s exactly why the revenue should be invested in their neighbourhoods. We already tax cigarettes and alcohol for similar reasons, and most people accept that. Nobody is banning soft drinks. The tax simply sends a signal that they should be an occasional treat, not something we drink every day with every meal.

scene.alt: A town square on a sunny day. In the centre stands an enormous red bicycle sculpture, about four times taller than a person and higher than the two-storey buildings on either side – a grey library on the left and an orange bakery on the right. A metal ladder leans against the bicycle’s frame, and a child in a yellow shirt is waving from partway up. In front, a sign reads “PEDAL POWER”. A man in a blue shirt points up at the bicycle while a woman in a purple dress takes a photo with a camera. On the right, a man in a green shirt holds up his phone beside a streetlamp. There is a bench on the left and a few clouds in the sky.

t8.prompt: You are on your town’s active-living committee. While visiting another city, you see this unusual attraction and think your town could build something similar. Call the committee chair, describe what you see, and explain whether you think your town should build something like it. The chair cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Hi Margot, it’s Sam. I’m in Westbrook for the weekend, and I’m standing in front of something you won’t believe. In the middle of the town square there’s a giant red bicycle – it’s taller than the two-storey buildings beside it. The wheels are as big as garage doors, and there’s a ladder leaning against the frame so kids can climb up toward the seat. A little boy is waving from halfway up, and there’s a sign in front that says “Pedal Power”. People are pointing and taking photos. I think we should propose something like this for our riverfront. It would attract visitors and get kids excited about cycling, which is exactly what our committee wants. My only concern is safety. That ladder looks steep, so we’d need soft padding underneath and maybe supervision on weekends. What do you think?
